blocks.x: My name is Esther Dupuis Breckenridge.
When was your born?
I was born in good old New Orleans on February the 25th, say 1906, that way back.
Have you lived in New Orleans all your life?
Mainly, I've traveled some, but this has been my headquarters all these many years.
When did you first come aware of the festival and the jazz?

Well, I first heard Ragtime, and I was very aware of music and was brought up in an atmosphere of music, taken to the opera very early in life, and we had all sorts of music. Naturally, when Ragtime came in, my father had that too. And I could remember the turkey trots and things like that. And then later on, when I was about 15 and 16 and started going to the fraternity dances, they had the Celestans Band, Piran, and all the good Dixieland jazz bands of the city. Gradually, as we grew up, in the debut parties and all the parties that I ever went to in New Orleans, we danced to jazz music.
And debut on parties, too.

Oh, yes. And private parties and other private parties, Tate-en-sons. The New Orleans Country Club had Tate-en-sons on Saturdays and Sundays, where they had the famous Perron himself. And he knew all of our crowd and the ones that were gifted and could dance and sing. And at all the parties, he would act as a sort of massive ceremonies and call on us to get up and do our stuff. We'd sing, harmonize, dance. You really don't see the young people do that as much as we used to, because that was a golden age of jazz. And we danced every night, you know, and in the daytime. We danced, I feel, more than the generations danced today.
What did your parents think of jazz? Your parents and their friends?

They were very interested in it. As I say, my father and mother belonged to a very musical crowd, and they were quite up-to-date. And they embraced that with any other music that happened to come along. They were interested in it and actually had big troller records for us with that music. And even had, we used to have groups of people to our house and have Perron over there to play for us. My father was always interested in listening to that music. He was a pianist himself. And he thought highly of their technique and was interested greatly in the movement.
And would you say he was interested in it as an art form for music? He had to come as entertainment.

Well, he was entertained by it, but my father went into anything in music more deeply than most people would for entertainment. And he really thought it was an era and something that would live. And he was very proud of the fact that it had mostly originated in his part of the world.
But his whole... Which part was it when you were born?
Oh, hey, what he was about... I imagined 30-something.
I think. When you were born? When I was born. So I would put him in... Maybe about 30. Put him in late 40s or early 70s.
No, not late 40s, did you say?
Late 40s or early 70s when you started going to parties and having parties that you have.
Oh, yes.
When can you remember his daughter having guys ran to the house or they used to...

Well, my father didn't necessarily have them. He just... He knew that we liked this group of Peron, and we had a crowd that would meet every Saturday and Sunday. He didn't actually ask them to come to the house, but he was interested when they were there. And if he was home, he was a doctor and was out of great deal. But whenever he was there, he listened very attentively to them and often had conversation with them on their different ideas of jazz because he was such a gifted pianist himself. And my sister was a very gifted pianist, and she was the best one who ever played jazz up at Newcomb. She had a concert of Gershwin, and she was a Gershwin exponent. I guess you could call Gershwin in the realm of jazz.
It's jazz, but not New Orleans.
Not New Orleans jazz, but...
Well, what did your parents' fans think of it? Did they universally like it, too?

They did. They did. Some of them were not as musical as my father. And... But they all condoned it. I mean, I don't have any recollection of any of them thinking it was... fresh. You know, they all... To my recollection, thought of it highly. Of course, we did, too. And I have... All your friends? Mm-hmm. As I say, we were a very dancing crowd. We sang and danced, and... Celestine was a hero to me. I mean, I can remember seeing him. I had been away a great deal, and I saw him about 12 years ago, and he hadn't seen me because he had been away, and it wasn't like the old days when he used to play at so many of the parties where I danced. And he said, um... Well, Miss Esther, he said, I've thought of you often, but I haven't seen you around, and I remember you and your sister harmonizing together. He said, And I thought maybe you had made the big-time stuff, and it's gotten on Broadway. And I said, Well, Celestine, no, I got married and had children instead. Not that I ever would have made the big-time stuff, but I said, That thing is a wonderful compliment coming from you to think that I could have, and we shook hands. And I thought very... So I went to his funeral, and God was... Being a member of the press, we were very near his coffin. It was a beautiful ceremony, very interesting, highly religious. And of course, the long line of people are all marching with the band. It was very impressive, but I think a great, great loss to New Orleans, and one that furthered jazz a great deal.
Well, among your friends, back in the 20s, did most of them just think of something to go dance to and have a good time to it? Did any of them...

Well, I'm afraid we... No, I... Harold Bartell was more interested in our craft than others, because he played the piano, and he played by ear like Steve, who was Perron's piano player, who was so well-known. And in fact, Steve gave him lessons, because he was interested in how. And I imagine... And of course, my sister and I, who sang a lot, were interested in the harmonizing part of it. But most of them, I would say, were not as devoted in jazz clubs as Menville and Soucha and all of them are today. It was so comparatively new that we accepted it as that and didn't realize what history it was making at the time.
What about... You know what you said, we didn't think of it as an art form.
Not to my regulation. I mean, we were all interested in learning. Learning it.
Yeah.
And following, but we had no idea that a real culture was being born right there in front of our eyes.
Well, you said that all the answers you all used to go to what... did have jazz bands. Do you know if it's blacking off at any time, having jazz bands and anything else? Jazz is supposed to...
Just be a fellow.
I guess it's a bit around the 30s or something like that.

I don't remember. It seems to me we always had very good colored bands down here. Most of the dances that I've ever been to up east. You know, when I went to those big debut parties up on Long Island, they had other the big name bands, Leo Reisman and all of those bands. But down here, I thought it really stuck pretty much to the colored bands. They had Johnny Detroit at some parties and was he at the Austin for a long time? Well, you wouldn't call him Dixieland Jazz, exactly.
No, No,
I know he was. He was a white band. And then the Owls, what were they? That particular name? Wasn't it?
I really don't know.
That was Benji White, Ebby Rowe, Guy Lyman, all those guys. Monk Steinman.
You met Mike Jazz?
Mm-hmm. Well, They were called the Owls, the group of white brothers.
And, you have all your life been going to the same debutante parties? Yes. And you've been all the time at the parties that did...

I never have remembered, even at the patio raw where most of our, you know, a lot of the debutante parties where we mostly had Pierron and Celestine. There might have been a time there where they had a few white bands, but if so, I wasn't conscious of it. You know, I mean, they weren't very good in my opinion and I don't even remember them.

What about, you know, the friends interested in it are other people who, do you know it's among white New Orleans interesting to be maintained throughout the years, during the 30s and the 40s? Whether they wanted it to remain? Mm-hmm. Well, I'd like to listen to it because they preferred to work for the rap because they were somewhat small communities.
I think they did. I think that we were, we thought it was here to stay, but we didn't realize how much of a, of an era, you know, that it was created. You wanted that to? know,
you said you were a member of the press, you were doing the society work, I think.

Yes, I had been several years before I was married, then I was married. I resigned, and then they needed someone temporarily, and I went back, and of course, on the news paper, it's very hard to get away from it, and I stayed and stayed.
How long have you been doing this?

Well, 30 years off and on, but I wouldn't, a great many of those years I haven't been on. More recently, I was on five years, so it has given me the opportunity through these years to have kept up pretty much with activities, even though it was past the age when I would have been going to debutante parties. So you have
been going to debutante parties every year?

Except during the war, I'd say when I was away most of the time, and I sometimes I went from the newspaper to cover it for pictures and things, and then sometimes friends of mine, their daughters would make their debut and I would go, and it seems to me the most popular form of music all through these years has been ambience and colored bands. Wouldn't you say?
I don't know about through the years, but you'd say that through the years it's maintained in it.
I would definitely say that. speaking for myself and speaking for all of my contemporaries and my daughter's contemporaries and through the ages, all the groups I've ever had to deal with.
You'd say your daughter's contemporary is like it too? Oh,
very much so.
And how old is your daughter?
She's 20 years old.
popularly forms of entertainment and dance here. Have you noticed any increase in interest in it as an art form? Oh,

yes, I think so. I mean, all over America and in England too. In New Orleans, I think the jazz club here is a very enthusiastic group. Harry Suchon, Edmond, Myra Menville and all that crowd. I've never been too active with them because I've been away a great deal since it was organized and was working on the paper, but I often covered their meetings to take pictures of them, and I thought their interest was very high and has increased all these years.
Would you say that you represented a majority of the only people that were incident in time?

I certainly would, and a different, you know, it covers all strata, young and old and from different walks of life all over New Orleans. I think it covers a larger establishment of people in New Orleans.

Well, then, you would say that over the, in some ways, you would say that over the years, as far as you know, people have liked it. I think it's an increase. Most New Orleans have liked it. Have liked it,
and I think gradually it is becoming in their eyes a form of art. And I think the Jazz Club has certainly increased that feeling among the people here.
Well,
they've had a chance to study it.
That start in the increase of interest as an art started, after the Second World War?

Yeah, well, I don't think it originated until then. And it has widened its membership each year and has increased the people in New Orleans to feel that it is art even now more than entertainment, which we had always thought. Because as I reiterate, they had a chance to study it in its various forms, which the are a to go to a one to a one to a !

average layman doesn't do, we just listen. But they have put a great deal, I mean, I'm sure that Dr. Sushaw has. I mean, he's been to a great many meetings all over the United States, and I imagine their meetings have whetted the appetite of a great many people to study it further in their club.
Well, over the years you say you can't remember any insightful amount of people thinking of it as trash or got a music there, or most people you have?
Most people. And I have always gone with a great many musical people on during my life, and I have never, to my knowledge, heard of anyone that thought about it as trash.
Do you think you have anything else to add on the line of social justice to the world

in jazz? I know I really don't, but I'm a joy being with you, and I wish that I had belonged to the Jazz Club all these years, because I would have been, had more at my fingertips to answer and to add to your little interview. And in fact, I think I will join, try to join up with the club now that I have more free time. Thank you very much.

segments.title: Introduction, birth and life in New Orleans
segments.summary: She gives her name, says she was born in New Orleans in 1906 and has mostly lived there.

segments.title: Ragtime, dances and Piron's band at society parties
segments.summary: Raised on opera and ragtime, she danced to Celestin, Piron and other bands at fraternity dances, debut parties and the Country Club, where Piron called on guests to perform.

segments.title: Her father and sister's interest in jazz
segments.summary: Her doctor father, a pianist, admired the technique of jazz players and thought it would live; her sister played Gershwin at Newcomb.

segments.title: Parents' friends' attitudes; Celestin as hero and his funeral
segments.summary: Friends all approved of jazz. She recalls Celestin's kind words when they met again and attending his funeral as a press member.

segments.title: Friends dancing to jazz without seeing it as art
segments.summary: Harold Bartell learned piano from Piron's pianist; most of her crowd enjoyed jazz without realizing a culture was being born.

segments.chapter: Jazz and society in New Orleans
segments.title: Bands at debutante parties: colored bands, Owls and others
segments.summary: New Orleans parties favored Black bands like Piron and Celestin, with some white bands such as Johnny DeDroit and the Owls.

segments.chapter: Jazz and society in New Orleans
segments.title: Whether white New Orleans kept its interest through the 30s and 40s
segments.summary: She thinks interest persisted, though they did not realize what an era it was.

segments.chapter: Jazz and society in New Orleans
segments.title: Her society newspaper work and decades of debutante parties
segments.summary: She worked the society beat on and off for about thirty years and says Black bands stayed most popular at debuts, including for her 20-year-old daughter's generation.

segments.title: Jazz Club and growing view of jazz as an art form
segments.summary: She credits the New Orleans Jazz Club with raising appreciation of jazz as art since the war, and says she never heard anyone call it trash.

segments.title: Closing remarks and thanks
segments.summary: She has nothing more to add, says she may join the Jazz Club, and thanks the interviewer.
